blocks.text: It is proved that ינשוף jansuph is the eagle owl.

Nor is it well enough known what ינשוף jansuph or jansoph is, the name of the bird that follows next. For, to pass over the Samaritans, who translate ࠁࠓࠁࠓࠉ barbari, that is, the Barbary bird, for what reason I do not know at all, I find four other interpretations of this word, very far removed from one another.

The first is that of the Greeks and of Jerome, who interpret it as ἶβιν [ibin], ibis, both here and at Esa. XXXIV, 11., where it is said of Idumaea: ינשוף Iansoph, and the raven shall dwell in it. Yet that passage plainly shows that jansoph is not the ibis. For the ibis is an Egyptian bird, as we know from Herodotus, Strabo, Pliny, Solinus and Ammianus. Εἰ δέ τις ἐπιθέμενος αὐτῇ τὸ καρτερὸν ἐξαγάγοι, ἣ δὲ ἀμύνεται τὸν ἐπιβουλεύσαντα, εἰς οὐδὲν αὐτῷ τὴν σπουδὴν προσαγαγοῦσα. ἑαυτὴν γὰρ ἀποκτείνει λιμῷ, καὶ ἀνόνητον τὴν προθυμίαν ἀποφαίνει τῷ προῃρημένῳ. [Ei de tis epithemenos autē to karteron exagagoi, hē de amynetai ton epibouleusanta, eis ouden autō tēn spoudēn prosagagousa. heautēn gar apokteinei limō, kai anonēton tēn prothymian apophainei tō proērēmenō.] But if anyone takes it away by force, it exacts punishment from the one who laid the snare, bringing his effort to nothing. For by starving itself to death it shows the attempt to be useless to the one who wanted it. These are the words of Aelian, [III, 25] History of Animals, book 2, chapter 38. Therefore there was no ibis in Idumaea. ^{(1)}.

The second version is that of the Syriac translator and of both Chaldees, that is, Jonathan and Onkelos, by whom the word is consistently rendered by the same word קפופא kiphupha, that is, eagle owl or little owl, as we proved from the Talmud in chapter 20, on the bird כוס thos. We shall say more about this version below.

The third is that of the Arabic translators of the Pentateuch, both of whom have here for ינשוף الباشق [al-bāshiq] albasak, a species of hawk, which Alkazuinius describes thus: طير احسن الصورة اصغر الجوارح جثة يصطاد العصافير [ṭayr aḥsan al-ṣūra aṣghar al-jawāriḥ juththa yaṣṭād al-ʿaṣāfīr], it is a bird most beautiful in appearance, and the smallest in body of the birds of prey, which hunts sparrows. This description fits the sparrowhawk, or sparverius. But Damir defines it very differently in the chapter On البازي [al-bāzī] albazi, or the hawk. There, namely, five species of hawks are given. 1. بازي [bāzī] bazi properly so called, which is named from its onrush ^{(2)}. 2. زرق [zurraq] zorrak, that is, blue-grey-eyed. 3. باشق [bāshiq] basak, so called in Arabic from its sharp sight, although most hold it to be Persian. 4. بيذق [baydhaq] [col. 282] that is, worthless. 5. عصفي [ʿaṣfī] asphi, that is, one that is carried into the middle of a whirlwind. Among these the basak is described thus: هو ايضا جار المزاج عليه القلق الزعارة يانس وقتا ويستوحش وقتا وهو قوي النفس فاذا انس منه الصغير بلغ صاحبه من صيده المراد وهو خفيف المحمل ظريف الشمايل يليق بالملوك ان تخدمه لانه يصيد افخر ما يصيده البازي وهو الدراج والحمام والورشان وهو كثير الشبق وهو قوي عليه صيده لا يتركه الي ان يتلف احدهما واجمل اوصافه ان يكون صغيرا في المنظر ثقيلا في الميزان طويل الساقين قصير الفخذين [huwa ayḍan jār al-mizāj ʿalayhi al-qalaq al-zaʿāra yaʾnas waqtan wa-yastawḥish waqtan wa-huwa qawī al-nafs fa-idhā anisa minhu al-ṣaghīr balagha ṣāḥibuhu min ṣaydihi al-murād wa-huwa khafīf al-maḥmil ẓarīf al-shamāʾil yalīq bi-l-mulūk an takhdumahu li-annahu yaṣīd afkhar mā yaṣīduhu al-bāzī wa-huwa al-durrāj wa-l-ḥamām wa-l-warashān wa-huwa kathīr al-shabaq wa-huwa qawī ʿalayhi ṣaydihi lā yatrukuhu ilā an yatlafa aḥaduhumā wa-ajmal awṣāfihi an yakūna ṣaghīran fī al-manẓar thaqīlan fī al-mīzān ṭawīl al-sāqayn qaṣīr al-fakhdhayn] It too is of a hot [III, 26] temperament, and therefore restless and of bad disposition, and sometimes it is tame, sometimes wild. Its breathing is strong. When it is tamed young, its master obtains his prey with a favourable wind. It is carried more easily and is clever by nature. Its use is most suited to kings, because it hunts nobler game than albazi, namely francolins, pigeons and turtledoves. It is very lustful. If it attacks a bird stronger than itself, it does not let it go until one of the two perishes. Most esteemed are those that are small in stature, heavy in weight, long in the shanks, short in the thighs ^{(3)}.
